h1: The 7 Best Mechanical Keyboards Under $100 for Typing, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 7 mechanical keyboards under $100 compared on mounting, hot-swap switches, keycaps, wireless modes and layout.
summary: The RK ROYAL KLUDGE R98 Pro is the best mechanical keyboard under $100, with a gasket mount, pre-lubed hot-swap switches and PBT keycaps. The AULA F99 is the best wireless pick, the Kisnt KN85 is the cheap 75% option, and the Redragon K671 is the best board for learning switches.
intro: Under $100, the keyboards that sound good are rarely the ones with the loudest listing. A cheap board with blue switches and a top-mounted plate rings like a typewriter, while a gasket board with foam and pre-lubed linears sounds muted and deep. Mounting style, not RGB count, decides whether you will enjoy the board in six months.

We reviewed seven mechanical keyboards from their listings, from wired budget units to tri-mode gasket boards. Three sit in the $50 to $100 band, near the top of the budget, and we flag them. Latency, battery and rating figures are manufacturer claims.

products.name: RK ROYAL KLUDGE R98 Pro Wired Mechanical Keyboard, 96% Gasket Mount
products.verdict: Gasket mount, pre-lubed cream linears and PBT keycaps in a wired 98-key layout.
products.description:
The R98 Pro keeps the numpad and arrow keys in a 98-key layout about 15.3 inches wide, which saves roughly an inch and a half over a full-size board. It uses a gasket mount with five cushioning layers, hot-swappable 3 or 5 pin sockets, pre-lubed cream linear switches, MDA profile double-shot PBT keycaps and a detachable aluminum volume knob.

It ranks first because it hands you the parts enthusiasts usually pay extra to upgrade: gasket mounting, factory lube and PBT caps. The wired connection avoids the battery and latency questions of wireless rivals, and the online driver handles remapping and macros on both Windows and Mac. It edges the AULA by being the better-sounding board in this price class, while the AULA wins on wireless freedom.

Buy it if you want a typing keyboard that sounds and feels refined without tinkering. Its price band is $50 to $100, so it is near the ceiling of this budget. The caveat is that cream linears suit people who like a smooth, quiet-ish press, not a clicky bump.
cons: Near the top of the budget
products.idealFor: Typists who want a refined, smooth board with a numpad.
products.skipIf: You want wireless or a clicky switch.

products.name: AULA F99 Wireless Mechanical Keyboard, Tri-Mode, Hot Swappable
products.verdict: Tri-mode connection, up to five paired devices and an 8000mAh battery.
products.description:
The F99 is a 99-key, 96% layout board with Bluetooth 5.0, 2.4GHz and USB-C wired modes, and it can hold up to five paired devices. It is hot-swappable for 3 and 5 pin switches, uses PBT keycaps and a gasket structure, and carries an 8000mAh battery. The kit includes a keycap puller and a switch puller.

It sits second because wireless adds a charge cycle and a small latency tradeoff that the wired R98 does not have. What you get back is flexibility, with one board shared across a laptop, a desktop and a tablet. The large battery is the strongest in this group, which matters for a board with RGB.

Buy it if you move between devices. Check the live price, since it sits in the $50 to $100 price band. The caveat is that the pre-lubed switches are linear, so typists who prefer tactile bumps will want to swap.
products.idealFor: Multi-device workers who want a numpad and wireless.
products.skipIf: You want a wired, zero-lag board.

products.name: SOLAKAKA A99 Pro Mechanical Keyboard with LCD Screen and Knob
products.verdict: A gasket board with a programmable LCD, metal knob and tri-mode wireless.
products.description:
The A99 Pro adds a small LCD screen and a metal knob to a gasket-mounted board with five layers of cushioning, PCB single-key slotting and noise-damping cotton. It is fully hot-swappable for 3 and 5 pin switches, runs 16 lighting modes plus side lights, and the web driver lets you set key mapping and even load a GIF on the screen.

It ranks third because the screen is a novelty to many typists, and every extra feature is one more thing to configure. It beats the Kisnt on layout and extras, but gives up some compactness. Nothing in the listing gives battery size, which the AULA states clearly.

Buy it if you like the idea of a status screen and a big knob. Skip it if you want a plain board. Its price band is $50 to $100.
products.idealFor: Enthusiasts who want a display and knob on a mid-priced board.
products.skipIf: You prefer a simple, no-software board.

products.name: Kisnt KN85 Wireless Mechanical Keyboard, 75%, Tri-Mode
products.verdict: An 85-key gasket board with listed latency figures and pre-lubed linear switches.
products.description:
The KN85 is a 75% layout with 85 keys, about 13.7 inches wide, that keeps the function row and arrows without a numpad. It supports USB-C, 2.4GHz and Bluetooth 5.0 with three channels, and lists latency of 2ms on USB, 5ms on 2.4GHz and 11ms on Bluetooth. Switches are pre-lubed linear, with 45 to 50gf actuation, hot-swappable on 3 or 5 pins.

It ranks fourth because dropping the numpad reduces it for anyone who enters data, but it frees about a quarter of desk space for the mouse. Publishing latency figures gives it more transparency than most. The listing warns against fast chargers, so use a normal 5V 1A source.

Buy it if you do not use a numpad. It falls in the $30 to $50 price band, so it is the least expensive wireless option here.
pros: Gasket mount for a soft thock
products.idealFor: Desk-minimalists who want wireless for the least.

products.name: Redragon K671 Mechanical Keyboard, Hot-Swappable Red Switch
products.verdict: A hot-swappable linear board that comes with four spare switches.
products.description:
The K671 uses hot-swappable linear red switches and comes with four spares, which lets you replace a failed switch without a soldering iron. It offers 11 backlight modes with five brightness levels, macro editing and key remapping, 12 multimedia shortcuts and anti-ghosting. The keycaps are double-injection ABS.

It sits fifth because it has no wireless, no gasket mount and ABS caps that shine with use. It does give hot-swap sockets at the lowest tier here, in the under $30 band, which is the best way to learn what switch you actually like.

Buy it if you want to experiment with switches without spending much. Skip it if you want a premium feel.
pros: Hot-swap sockets at a low price
products.idealFor: First-time hobbyists who want to try switches.
products.skipIf: You want wireless or a gasket feel.

products.name: Redragon K582 Wired RGB Mechanical Keyboard, 104-Key
products.verdict: A standard 104-key linear red board rated for 50 million keystrokes.
products.description:
The K582 is a full-size 104-key layout with linear red switches, N-key rollover, 18 backlight modes over 6 themes, programmable keys and companion software. The listing rates it for 50 million keystrokes and a gold-plated USB connector.

It ranks sixth because the switches are not hot-swappable, so the feel is whatever you start with. For anyone who needs a full numpad and a reliable, no-fuss board, it works. It is in the $30 to $50 price band.

Buy it if you want a standard layout and a long rated life. Skip it if you want to customize switches.
products.idealFor: People who want a conventional full-size mechanical board.
products.skipIf: You want to swap switches later.

products.name: Meidosa AK96 Mechanical Keyboard, 96%, Blue Switches, Hot Swap
products.verdict: A clicky 96% board with PBT keycaps, a knob and dual-side lighting.
products.description:
The AK96 is a top-mount 96% board with blue switches, PBT keycaps, a knob and 17 RGB modes with dual-side LEDs. Switches are hot-swappable, the connection is USB-C wired, and two kickstands plus rubber pads set the typing angle.

It comes last because blue switches are loud and a top-mount plate transmits more bounce than a gasket build. It does offer clicky feedback and a numpad at the lowest tier, in the under $30 price band.

Buy it if you like an audible click and do not share a room. Skip it for open offices.
pros: PBT keycaps at a low price
products.idealFor: Fans of tactile, audible switches on a budget.

methodology.description: Mounting style, keycap material and plate design were compared, since these set sound and feel.

methodology.title: Switch type and swap support
methodology.description: We checked switch type, lubing and whether sockets are hot-swappable.

methodology.title: Connectivity
methodology.description: Wired and tri-mode boards were scored on latency data, battery size and pairing options.

methodology.title: Layout fit
methodology.description: Full-size, 96%, 98-key and 75% layouts were weighed against desk space and numpad needs.

methodology.title: Value inside $100
methodology.description: Five of seven picks cost less than $100 by their bucket, and the three in the $50 to $100 band are flagged as near the top.

whatMatters.detail: A gasket mount floats the plate on foam, giving a softer, deeper sound. A top mount screws the plate to the case and feels stiffer. Listings say gasket structure or top mount, and gasket boards are what to choose if you type all day.

Linear switches go straight down, tactile switches have a bump, and clicky ones add a sound. Pre-lubed linears feel smooth out of the box. If you are unsure, pick a hot-swap board so you can change your mind.

Sockets let you pull switches without soldering, which means a failed key is a thirty-second fix. Look for 3 or 5 pin support, and a switch puller in the box. Non-hot-swap boards lock you into the starter switch.
PBT keycaps resist shine and have a textured feel, while ABS wears glossy within months. Double-shot caps keep legends from fading. Boards that list PBT usually cost slightly more, and are worth it.

Wired is the simplest and has the lowest latency, while 2.4GHz is close behind and Bluetooth is slowest. The Kisnt lists 2ms, 5ms and 11ms for the three modes. If you game competitively, prefer wired or 2.4GHz.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A gasket mount, linear or tactile switches rather than clicky ones, and PBT keycaps that resist shine.

cards.label: In this ranking
cards.text: R98 Pro is the quietest-feeling, and the Kisnt and AULA add wireless.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You want an aluminum case, a proven brand or software that goes beyond remapping. Those are in the $150 and up bracket.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You want to learn what you like. The Redragon K671 lets you swap switches.

faq.q: Do these work on a Mac?
faq.a: Most list Windows and macOS compatibility, and the RK driver explicitly supports both. Check the Fn row for media keys, since Mac key labels differ.
Buying clicky blue switches for a shared home. Blue switches are loud, so choose linear or tactile if others can hear you.

faq.q: Is the R98 Pro worth it over the AULA F99?
faq.a: If you stay at one desk, yes, since it is wired and tuned for sound. If you move between devices, the AULA's tri-mode connection is worth the premium.
Remove the keycap, grip the switch with the puller and lift it straight out. Insert the new switch with its pins aligned and push until it seats.

faq.q: How do I keep it clean?
faq.a: Pull keycaps every few months and blow out dust. PBT caps can be washed in mild soap and dried fully.
Bluetooth adds a little, and 2.4GHz is nearly wired. The Kisnt lists 2ms, 5ms and 11ms for the three modes.

finalTake: The RK ROYAL KLUDGE R98 Pro is the best mechanical keyboard under $100 for most typists, thanks to its gasket mount, factory lube and PBT keycaps. The AULA F99 earns the wireless slot, and the Kisnt KN85 is the cheap compact choice. If you are new to switches, the Redragon K671 is the cheapest way to find out what you like.
